rv.q: Those politics make “What Became of Us” a highly topical play, if a frustrating one in Jennifer Chang’s production for Atlantic Theater Company.

I typically detest this style of theater, which so often feels like a negation of the dramatic form . But Lotfi’s text stealthily shifts direction so that speech at seamlessly transforms into speech with as this sibling relationship evolves.
What Became of Us has charming and warm moments, but lacks the imagination and spark of Home .

What Became of Us is a beautiful meditation on the life and offers up a unique theatregoing experience with its double casting, but the heightened language and lack of dialogue exchange slow the pace.
It's an often engaging, sometime poignant look at the evolution of a sibling relationship, colored by the older sister having been born abroad, the brother born after their parents immigrated.

By artfully elevating a familiar saga of immigrant families with forceful wordplay, fondly wrapping it in brother and sister ties, and leaving identity markers open, the author provides a gently touching work of universal appeal.
